cards.title: Admission and CEL
items: Connect mode was shipped with provision deliberately closed. The webhook and the CEL rules both reject it today, and this epic is what opens them.
The relaxation is additive and sits behind a new gate. With the gate off, a provision-mode object is rejected with a message that names the gate.
adopt stays rejected either way, so the mode triad is still only two thirds open after this lands.

cards.title: Hub API server
items: SpokeCluster grows spec.provider and spec.infraProvisioning.blueprintRef, plus a status tree carrying per-plane and per-component state and outputs.
The phase machine is Pending, Provisioning, Ready, Failed, with startedAt and an estimated completion so a long create is legible while it runs.
Three CRDs arrive alongside it: ClusterProviderDefinition, ClusterPlane and ClusterBlueprint. All three exist today only as KEP text.

cards.title: Provision controller
items: Runs on the hub and needs no connectivity to the spoke, because at the point it starts there is no spoke to reach.
It resolves the provider definition, reconciles the infraProvisioning blueprint, then translates cloud states such as CREATING and ACTIVE into the phase machine.
A mid-provision failure names the failing component in a condition and one event, keeps what was already created, and converges on retry without manual cloud cleanup.

cards.title: ClusterBlueprint and ClusterPlane
items: The blueprint composes planes and orders them with dependsOn. The plane controller runs the components inside one plane and publishes its outputs.
Outputs are the ordering mechanism. A component whose upstream output is missing stays Pending with a condition naming the unmet dependency instead of failing.
No EKS call happens before vpcId and the private subnets exist, and no node group call happens before the cluster reports ACTIVE.

cards.title: Crossplane
items: The only backend implemented. The provider definition keeps schematic arms for CAPI, tf-controller, ACK and KRO in the schema, with nothing behind them.
The AWS providers are already installed and enabled in Atmos, serving data-service compositions. Nothing has pointed them at cluster-shaped infrastructure yet.
The provider role needs VPC, IAM and EKS create rights. That is a real privilege expansion over today's scope and needs a security review, not a broad grant.

cards.title: Shared prereq and per-cluster
items: The prereq plane builds the VPC, three availability zones of subnets, NAT and IGW, the cluster IAM roles and the OIDC provider, with the Kubernetes ELB subnet tags.
A second SpokeCluster naming the same blueprint consumes those outputs rather than building a second VPC, and the plane lists both consumers.
A consumer-check finalizer refuses to delete a shared plane while anything still consumes it, and names the consumers in the refusal. Terraform state layout gives this only by convention.

cards.title: cluster-gateway handoff
items: Provision ends where connect begins. Connectivity is derived from plane outputs, so there is no static kubeconfig anywhere in this path.
The Secret uses the contract connect mode already established, which is why vela cluster list and topology policies work against a provisioned cluster with no change.
The bare-minimum target is a private endpoint, IRSA, and one small system node group. No add-on stack, no Flux bootstrap, no Atmos NG parity.

cards.title: Teardown and what is left out
items: Cleanup runs in reverse phase order and is checked against the cloud account, so no VPC, NAT gateway, IAM role, OIDC provider or node group is left orphaned.
Re-applying an unchanged specification makes no mutating cloud call, and the reconcile rate is measured so amplification is detectable.
Out of scope: provisioning the hub, the rollout engine, drift detection, revision publishing, non-AWS providers, and replacing Terraform as the Atmos path.
